data.text:
A correction to the reason on record 230, which lost a clause to the shell before it was
written, and a note on the habit that keeps causing it.

The sentence should read: written as an author avoiding the guard would, as
  const fs: any = await vi.importActual('node:fs');
it reports only ["vitest"], which is allow-listed as handing a test no way to open a path.

What happened is that the clause was wrapped in backticks inside a double-quoted shell
argument, so zsh tried to expand it and dropped it. The record now says "written as an
author avoiding the guard would, , it reports only", with the spelling that is the whole
point of F47 missing from it. The journal is append-only and record 230 stands as written;
this note is where the sentence lives.

That is the third time this session that a backtick inside a double-quoted shell string has
eaten authored text: twice in a commit message, once here. The first was caught because the
commit could be amended before it was pushed, the second because the message was re-read
afterwards, and this one because the shell printed its complaint. None of them was caught by
intent. The rule that would have prevented all three is to pass prose through a file or a
heredoc rather than through an argument, which is what every harness note in this ticket
already does and what the `--reason` flag does not offer.

## What F47 is, restated so the journal carries it once correctly

`packages/core/db/repository.ts` allows `vitest` in `IMPORTS_THAT_CANNOT_READ` on the stated
ground that the test runner "hands a test no way to open a path". That is false.
`vi.importActual` takes a literal specifier, and `ts.preProcessFile` does not report it, so a
module of this package can obtain `node:fs` or `node:child_process` while `readingImportsOf`
returns nothing and the guard that exists to make the reader unavoidable says the package is
clean. `rls.test.ts` already imports `vi`, so the hazard is one line from a module that
exists.

Measured here before the finding was recorded, and one false negative of my own is worth
recording with it. Written with `typeof import('node:fs')` in a type position, the
pre-processor does report `node:fs`, because a type-only import is still an import to it, and
my first probe therefore said the guard was fine. Removing the type annotation, which is what
an author avoiding the guard would do, leaves only `["vitest"]`. The lesson is the one this
ticket keeps producing: a probe that includes a construct the guard handles proves nothing
about the construct it does not.

It is also F44's shape one round after F44: a stated impossibility that is false, sitting in
a list the module presents as complete. The module names three survivals, a computed
specifier, `createRequire` other than through `node:module`, and `eval`. This is a fourth,
with a literal specifier, and a lint rule would miss it too.
